raw_response:
I am 64 years old and have worked these 10.1 mu in Quzhou for 38 years. With only two mouths to feed at home now, I do not need to chase extreme yields, but I must farm steadily without wearing myself out. My well gives me water, but pumping costs electricity, so I irrigate only when the crops truly need it.

I keep 8 mu in my wheat-maize rotation because it is reliable: the wheat is already in the ground, and I know that three irrigations in spring—green-up, jointing, and filling—will carry it to about 500 kg per mu. I use improved wheat seed and give it a moderate dose of fertilizer; at my age I have learned that more nitrogen does not always mean more grain. For the summer maize, I will plant hybrid seed directly into the wheat stubble without ploughing. No-tillage saves me seven to ten days between harvest and planting, and with only two of us, those days matter. Two irrigations for the maize are usually enough if the summer rains are normal, and I expect around 580 kg per mu.

The remaining 2.1 mu I plant to cotton. It brings in cash, but it is fussy work—thinning, pruning, and picking all by hand. I use an improved cotton seed I trust, till the soil with the rotary tiller in spring, and irrigate three times. Cotton pests never sleep, so I spray four times, no more and no less. I hope for 85 kg of seed cotton per mu. If the price is fair, it is worth the extra labor; if not, I may reduce the cotton next year. But for now, this is the balance that keeps my household fed and solvent.
